doc.title: Clyde Kerr Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006

title: Teaching young players to find their own voice; Nicholas Payton, Christian Scott
summary: The hardest thing is students copying others; he avoids teaching licks and mentions students Nicholas Payton and Christian Scott.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Is that the hardest part — well let me rephrase — what’s the hardest part for you to teach to younger players about improvising or music in general?

The hardest part. Well one of the things that was hard was that a lot of the young musicians were losing their own identity and copying the style and the notes that other musicians were playing in the beginning. So I would tell them I’d say it’s great, man, what you’re doing, but it’s a time where you have to let that go and start trying to get your own voice, your own style. And some of them still to this day still haven’t gotten away from copying whoever they were listening to at the particular time to find their own voice and their own style. I mean you have to do that sometimes to get to where you want to get, but you’ve got to know when to hold ‘em and when to fold ‘em like. You know? And for me, like I said, I was just so fortunate I had so much experiences, not only just with the music thing but my life in general. Because I don’t draw just from my musical experience I draw from my whole life and try to bring it together. And I always talk about the point. The point is the time that you’re in right now, the moment. So this right now, we are at this point of our lives, all three of us here. And so from that we are bringing our experience of who we were yesterday and the day before that to this moment. And from that you can react to certain things because you have that history to draw from. And that’s what I used to try to teach those kids who didn’t know when to let it go and say okay well I got that, okay let me see what I can do with it to make it mine, to make it sound like — if I would given them an idea. Because I never did like to teach cliches or licks as we call them. I would use certain things as a means to getting to other things. You know say okay, I will give you this. Okay now let me see what you’re going to do with it. Some of them would take it and develop it and turn it around so much that I wouldn’t even recognize it myself which, that’s the purpose. Some of them are still playing the things the way I gave it to them. Like I taught Nicholas Payton as a young musician. He is at home in East New Orleans right now. We were still talking and man he’s taking, gone, and it’s his now. And another great musician as a young trumpet player, Christian Scott, he’s out there, he just has a brand new CD out, trumpet player. But a lot of people associate me with just teaching trumpet players but I had trumpets, piano players, bass players, guitar players, you know. And they’re all like family. And a lot of them still keep in touch after so many years.
